Consult Summary:
- First episode of acute left-sided headache with visual aura and vomiting starting this morning; clinical picture most consistent with migraine with visual aura. Same-day in-person neurologic assessment planned to confirm and exclude secondary causes.

History:
- Presenting complaint/timeline:
  - Sudden-onset left-sided headache started this morning (~4 hours before consult); intensity ~6/10.
  - Visual disturbance: blurred vision with “zigzag lines” (ongoing, slightly improved); cannot tolerate screens.
  - Associated: dizziness, nausea, two episodes of vomiting at onset; worse with movement; prefers head still.
  - Analgesia: paracetamol taken ~3 hours after onset with no relief.
  - No prior similar headaches.
- Pertinent negatives mentioned:
  - No limb weakness; walking is normal.
  - Denies typical retro-orbital pain; not clearly behind the eye.
- Past medical history: Kidney stones.
- Family history: Mother with migraines; hypothyroidism in family.
- Medications: None.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Social/preventive: Pregnancy considered unlikely. Other social history not discussed.

Examination:
- No vitals documented.
- No physical exam performed (teleconsult).
- Neurologic symptoms by history: No focal deficits reported; gait normal.

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Migraine with visual aura (most likely).
  - Supporting: Unilateral headache; visual zigzag lines/blurred vision; screen intolerance; nausea/vomiting; family history of migraine; no focal deficits by history.
  - Notes: Described as sudden onset; aura persisting for several hours is less typical but can occur.
- Important differentials to consider/exclude:
  1) Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) – medium concern given first sudden-onset headache with vomiting at onset; absence of focal deficits and pain not “worst ever” lowers likelihood but does not exclude.
  2) Cervical artery dissection – low likelihood; unilateral acute headache and dizziness without neck pain/trauma or focal signs.
  3) Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) – low likelihood; risk factors not elicited; presentation more consistent with migraine.

Plan:
- Acute treatment (per discussion):
  - Trial ibuprofen with an over-the-counter anti-sickness medication (from pharmacy).
  - Drink a sugary, carbonated beverage (e.g., cola) as advised.
  - If inadequate relief, consider escalation to specific migraine-relief medication (per GP follow-up).
- Follow-up and assessment:
  - Same-day in-person appointment arranged for full neurologic examination; if symptoms resolve substantially before the appointment after treatment, patient may cancel.
- Safety-net/when to seek urgent care (added given first sudden severe headache and DDx considerations):
  - Go to emergency care if any red flags occur: sudden “worst headache of life,” rapidly worsening headache, new neurological deficits (weakness, speech difficulty, confusion), persistent/refractory vomiting, neck stiffness, loss of consciousness, or visual loss.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements:
  - Vitals (BP, HR, temp), full neurologic and ocular exam, neck stiffness assessment.
  - Detailed headache characterization (exact thunderclap timing to peak, photophobia/phonophobia confirmation, triggers), recent head/neck trauma, anticoagulant use, infectious symptoms/fever, medication doses, caffeine use, oral contraceptive use, smoking history, postpartum status, coagulation history.
  - Pregnancy test not performed (pregnancy “unlikely” only by history).
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - DDx flags SAH as a medium concern due to sudden onset and vomiting; transcript management focused on migraine treatment with same-day clinic assessment rather than immediate emergency evaluation. Conflict noted regarding urgency.
  - DDx notes typical aura lasts 5–60 minutes; patient’s visual disturbance persisted for several hours. Conflict noted.
● Transcript quality:
  - Teleconsult with intermittent connection issues; limited ROS and no physical exam or vitals; some answers truncated/uncertain.
